findings.quote: A bigger speed or a smaller circle means a larger $a_c$.
findings.problem: The claim that a smaller circle gives a larger centripetal acceleration holds only at the same speed, and the sentence does not say so. At the same angular speed it is false: $a_c=\omega^2r$ grows with $r$. The lesson itself later says that on a rigid spinning object, points farther from the axis have a larger $a_c$ (riders A and B in #6: A has the smaller circle and the smaller $a_c$). A student asked whether a point near the rim or near the center of a spinning disk has the larger centripetal acceleration gets two opposite answers from the lesson.
findings.source: Checklist B01 and reader rules, Added after the Sol audit (boundary test); $a_c=v^2/r=\omega^2r$, OpenStax College Physics 2e, 6.2 Centripetal Acceleration

findings.quote: Then add up the parts of the real forces that point toward the center. That sum equals $mv^2/r$.
findings.problem: The method counts only force parts that point toward the center. When a real force has an outward part, it must be subtracted. At the bottom of a swing or vertical circle the rule gives $T=mv^2/r$ instead of $T-mg=mv^2/r$; at the top of a hill crest it gives $mg=mv^2/r$ instead of $mg-N=mv^2/r$. The same false rule is repeated in Speed Tricks: "find which real forces have a part toward the center. Their sum equals $mv^2/r$". The base said "net radial component", which was right. The lesson's own sentence just above calls it the net force toward the center, so the procedure contradicts it.
findings.source: Checklist B01; Newton's second law along the radius, OpenStax College Physics 2e, 6.3 Centripetal Force; reader rules, Added after the Sol audit

findings.quote: For a launch from a height onto lower ground, the angle for the longest range is a bit less than $45^\circ$.
findings.problem: How far the best angle drops below $45^\circ$ depends on the height compared with $v_0^2/g$; it is not always a bit less. For the lesson's own Example #4 ($10$ m/s from a $15$ m cliff), the best angle satisfies $\tan\theta=v_0/\sqrt{v_0^2+2gh}=10/\sqrt{394}$, so $\theta\approx27^\circ$, about $18^\circ$ below $45^\circ$. The general statement fails for the case the trap itself points to.
findings.source: Checklist B01; standard result for maximum range from a height, $\tan\theta_{\text{best}}=v_0/\sqrt{v_0^2+2gh}$, checked by solving

findings.problem: The formula $f_{s,\max}=\mu_sN$ and the term coefficient of static friction appear for the first time inside Example #8. Core Concept never gives them, and the lesson names no prerequisite lesson for them (the brief's prior knowledge lists real-force identification, not the friction coefficient). The example question also asks for $\mu_s$ before the student has met it. A student without the dynamics lesson cannot follow step 2 or answer the question.
findings.source: Checklist L17 (every formula appears in Core Concept before any example uses it) and L25; brief, Necessary prior knowledge
